candidates.source_description: Cartonnage mask in the form of a jackal head, possibly dating to the Graeco-Roman Period (332 BC–395 AD). The mask is made of layers of linen, stiffened with plaster and then painted. It is painted black with white/yellow stripes. Red paint has been used for the eyes and mane. The mask has been heavily restored in modern times with parts of it now missing. Anubis was the ancient Egyptian god of embalming and so it is possible that this mask was worn by an embalmer during the mummification process, particularly the opening of the mouth ritual. In fact, the Abusir Papyrus lists the presence of an Anubis mask amongst the priestly objects in the temple of Raneferef. Documentary evidence shows that the use of an Anubis mask for religious purposes existed since at least the Old Kingdom, or even earlier. From microscopic examples taken by scientists at the University of York, we know that the paint on the mask is made from castor oil and olive oil mixed with animal fat and conifer resin.

Visible on the left side of the fragment is Bes' thick, heavily incised leonine mane, rendered with deep vertical grooving, alongside his widely extended, flat protruding tongue. candidates.source_description: A small magical stela, known as a cippus, carved from steatite (soapstone). The front of the stela features a high-relief depiction of the child god Horus (Harpakhered), who is represented naked with the traditional sidelock of youth hanging on the right side of his head. He stands triumphantly atop at least one crocodile, grasping a collection of dangerous desert fauna—including scorpions and snakes—in his outstretched hands to demonstrate his absolute mastery over chaotic and venomous forces. Directly above his head is the heavily abraded face of the protective dwarf deity Bes, acting as a secondary guardian element. The reverse side and the narrow outer edges of the stela are densely covered with incised columns of hieroglyphic protective spells. The entire surface of the stone shows significant mechanical wear, smoothing out many of the finer textual and anatomical details. It dates from the Late Period to Graeco-Roman Period (c. 664–30 BC).

Her pose, standing with her hands extending outward as if she were holding something, is typical of the corn goddess Chicomecoatl. A sculpture like this one would have been the focal point of a shrine.
